data.originalText: Plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar through photosynthesis. Chlorophyll captures light energy in the leaves. Roots absorb water from the soil, while tiny openings in leaves take in carbon dioxide. The plant stores some sugar and releases oxygen into the air.

readingLevel.explanation: Short sentences and explicit cause-and-effect relationships support upper-elementary readers.

data.def: The process plants use to make sugar from light, water, and carbon dioxide.
data.example: Photosynthesis lets a plant store the Sun's energy in sugar.

data.def: The green material in leaves that captures light energy.
data.example: Chlorophyll makes most leaves look green.

data.def: A gas from the air that plants use to build sugar.
data.example: Leaves take in carbon dioxide through tiny openings.

data.def: A gas released by plants during photosynthesis and used by many living things.
data.example: The plant releases oxygen into the air.

data.def: A simple sugar plants make and use for energy and growth.
data.example: A plant can store glucose for later.

data.def: To take in or soak up a substance or energy.
data.example: Roots absorb water from the soil.

data.def: To let something move out or become available.
data.example: Leaves release oxygen into the air.

data.def: The ability to cause change or make things happen.

data.title: Build-a-Leaf Relay
data.description: Teams carry input cards—sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide—to a leaf model, then trade them for glucose and oxygen output cards. Students narrate each exchange using the process vocabulary.
data.connection: Makes the movement of matter and transfer of energy visible and physical.
data.guide: Place input cards at three stations. Require the runner to explain what each input contributes before receiving an output card.
data.worksheet: Draw the leaf station. Label each input and output. In two sentences, explain where the energy begins and where it is stored.

data.title: Sunlight Investigation
data.description: Compare two identical plants or leaf samples placed in different light conditions. Students predict, observe, and record evidence over several days.
data.connection: Connects the abstract role of sunlight to observable changes in living plants.
data.guide: Keep water, plant type, and container size the same. Discuss why a fair test changes only one variable.
data.worksheet: Write your prediction, record one observation each day, and use evidence to explain whether light affected the plant.

data.title: Photosynthesis Comic Strip
data.description: Students create a six-panel comic that follows a water droplet and carbon dioxide molecule as they enter a plant, become part of sugar, and release oxygen.
data.connection: Uses narrative and drawing to reinforce sequence, plant structures, and conservation of matter.
data.guide: Require every panel to include one accurate science label and one cause-and-effect caption.
data.worksheet: Plan six panels: roots, stem, leaf, chlorophyll, glucose, and oxygen. Add arrows to show movement.

data.title: How Scientists Explained Photosynthesis
data.historicalContext: For centuries, people wondered how plants gained mass and stayed alive. Scientists gradually used controlled observations to show that plants take in matter from water and air and use light energy to make sugar.

documents.title: Document A: Van Helmont's Willow Tree
documents.source: Adapted classroom account of Jan Baptista van Helmont's experiment, 1600s
documents.excerpt: Van Helmont planted a young willow tree in a measured amount of dry soil. For five years he added only water. The tree gained a great deal of mass, while the soil's mass changed very little. He concluded that much of the new plant material came from water, although later scientists showed that carbon dioxide from the air also supplied matter.

happPrompts.historical: What did people know about plant growth in the 1600s?
happPrompts.audience: Who might learn from this experiment?
happPrompts.purpose: Why did Van Helmont measure both the tree and the soil?
happPrompts.pointOfView: How did the evidence shape his conclusion?

sourcingQuestions: Which parts of the investigation were measured?
analysisQuestions: What did the evidence support, and what important input was still missing from the explanation?

documents.title: Document B: Priestley's Sealed Jar
documents.source: Adapted classroom account of Joseph Priestley's experiments, 1770s
documents.excerpt: Priestley observed that a flame soon went out in a sealed jar. A mouse also could not survive for long in the same closed air. When he placed a green plant in the jar and waited, the air could again support a flame. The plant had changed the air, but the exact role of light was not yet clear.

happPrompts.historical: What tools were available to study gases in the 1770s?
happPrompts.audience: Who would be interested in evidence about air?
happPrompts.purpose: Why compare jars with and without a plant?
happPrompts.pointOfView: What could Priestley observe directly, and what did he infer?

sourcingQuestions: What comparison made this a useful investigation?
analysisQuestions: How does this evidence connect plants to oxygen?
sentenceStarters: The plant changed the air because...

documents.title: Document C: Ingenhousz Tests Light
documents.source: Adapted classroom account of Jan Ingenhousz's experiments, 1779
documents.excerpt: Ingenhousz placed aquatic plants in clear containers and compared what happened in sunlight and darkness. In light, bubbles formed around the green parts of the plants. In darkness, the bubbles stopped. He concluded that light was necessary for green plants to release the gas that later scientists identified as oxygen.

happPrompts.historical: How did this experiment build on earlier work about plants and air?
happPrompts.pointOfView: How did visible bubbles influence the conclusion?

sourcingQuestions: What was the independent variable in this investigation?
analysisQuestions: Why are the results stronger because both light and darkness were tested?
sentenceStarters: The comparison supports the claim that...

history.title: Photosynthesis - Grade 5 adaptation
history.data:
## Photosynthesis

Plants make their own food. Leaves capture energy from sunlight. Roots bring in water, and leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air. The plant uses these materials to make sugar for energy. Oxygen is released back into the air.
